newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vienna auction house accused of selling fakes.
newsitem.headline: Vienna auction house accused of selling fakes.

text.p: Vienna's venerable Dorotheum, the world's second oldest auction house, is struggling to save face after admitting it wrongly labelled some objects as oriental antiques which one expert described as "pure junk."

The Dorotheum, seeking to quell a growing chorus of criticism over a controversial Asiatica fine arts auction earlier this month, brought in leading Asiatica experts to investigate a number of disputed catalogue entries.
"Over 100 objects were what I would call pure junk," one of the experts, Johannes Wieninger of Vienna's Museum for Applied Arts (MAK), told Reuters on Friday.
The state-owned auction house, established in 1785, said the findings of the investigation had led it to stop holding any more Asiatica auctions.
"The current state of the investigation does indicate.... that the labelling of some catalogue positions was incorrect or not exact," it said in a statement.
"This does not represent the style of the Dorotheum as a renowned auction house and is therefore unacceptable," it said.
Wieninger, the MAK's East Asia expert, said sculptures labelled in the catalogue as Japanese netsuke miniatures were quite obviously modern Chinese reproductions.

He also claimed it took just one glance at items labelled as shunga -- erotic prints by 18th century Japanese wood-block artists -- to see that they did not belong to traditional iconography. Instead, Wieninger said, they were aimed at the "erotic preferences of Western sex tourists".
Wieninger was alerted to the inauthenticity as shunga usually appear fairly innocuous at first glance and only closer inspection reveals their true erotic significance.
He also claimed that various articles of furniture in the auction were in fact new.
The Austrian Association of Antiques and Art Dealers said on Friday the Asiatica scandal had inflicted severe damage on the Austrian art market.

It demanded in a statement that, "to restore the confidence of the consumer," the Dorotheum and other auction houses must undertake to give cast iron guarantees of the correctness of their catalogue details.
